analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying forever and extends staff lobbying bans.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan lobbying-ban bill was referred to a Senate committee on May 18, 2017, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have imposed a lifetime ban on former senators, representatives, and elected congressional officers lobbying Congress — up from the current two-year ban for senators and one year for House members. It would have stretched the cooling-off period for most congressional staff from one year to six, barred registered lobbyists from taking congressional jobs with offices they had lobbied for six years after their contacts, forced large lobbying firms to disclose which former members and senior staff they pay, and raised the maximum penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000. It also directed creation of a searchable public website, lobbyists.gov, for lobbying disclosures.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to know who is paid to influence the laws that govern them. The bill would have made it harder for former lawmakers and senior aides to turn their congressional connections into lobbying jobs, and easier for the public to see which firms employ former members of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the lobbying ban for former House members and senators to a lifetime, with criminal penalties under section 216 of title 18 for violations [S3].
Raises the post-employment lobbying restriction from one year to six years for congressional staff, committee staff, leadership staff, and other legislative employees [S2].

Bars registered lobbyists and foreign-principal agents from being hired by any member or committee they substantially lobbied for six years, with a narrow waiver only for compelling national need [S3].

Requires large lobbying firms — those employing more than three registered lobbyists — to file annual lists of former members of Congress and highly paid former legislative officials they hire or retain as consultants, and sends those filings to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to check for underreporting [S3].
Increases the civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000 and directs a searchable public database, lobbyists.gov [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms, law and government-relations practices, and the former members of Congress and senior staff who sell their access and knowledge of the legislative process to them. Firms would lose a recruiting pipeline; ex-lawmakers would lose a lucrative second career.
analysis.who_pays_short: K Street lobbying firms and former lawmakers

drawbacks.text: The six-year hiring ban on former lobbyists cuts both ways: it can also bar congressional offices from hiring people with genuine subject-matter expertise in the areas they lobbied, potentially pushing offices to rely on less-qualified staff [S3].
The waiver for the lobbyist-hiring ban depends on congressional ethics committees finding a 'compelling national need,' giving those committees discretion that could blunt the rule in practice [S3].

Defining 'substantial lobbying contact' is inherently fuzzy — the bill excludes simple social contacts but relies on judgment calls about meetings, fundraising participation, and earmark solicitation, which invites disputes and enforcement gaps [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest: slightly thinner hiring pools for congressional offices and some enforcement ambiguity. The benefit is structural — lawmakers would no longer be able to preview, however implicitly, a lifetime lobbying career funded by the industries they regulate. The main honest objection is that a lifetime ban may exceed what is needed, since a long cooling-off period can capture most of the access value without permanently restricting former officials' livelihoods.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee from the day it was introduced until Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the bill on May 18, 2017, joined by Republican Senator Cory Gardner and Democratic Senator Al Franken [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — was ever recorded for the bill in the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and former members of Congress, who keep the existing one- and two-year revolving-door rules and the current $200,000 disclosure penalty. The status quo — short cooling-off periods, limited disclosure — was preserved because the bill never moved.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never received floor action or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — one Democrat and one Republican cosponsored it alongside its Democratic sponsor — but it never reached a vote, so no vote breakdown exists; its death was a committee inaction rather than a party-line defeat.

industries.note: The bill would have cut off their main recruiting pipeline — former members and senior staff with current relationships on Capitol Hill — and forced firms with more than three lobbyists to publicly disclose the ex-lawmakers they pay. The bill's death preserves that pipeline.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress selling lobbying and consulting services
industries.note: A lifetime lobbying ban would have ended the well-documented practice of ex-lawmakers monetizing their congressional connections, and firms would have had to list them publicly. The bill never advanced, so this market is unchanged.
